veer.e: Borrowed from Middle Dutch vieren (“to slacken”).
veer.g: To let out (a sail-line), to allow (a sheet) to run out.
A turn or swerve; an instance of veering.

vegetable.e: From Middle English vegetable, from Old French vegetable, from Latin vegetābilis (“able to live and grow”), derived from vegetāre (“to enliven”).

vegetation.e: Borrowed from Middle French végétation, from Medieval Latin vegetātiōnem.

vehement.e: Borrowed from Middle French vehement (modern French véhément; compare Italian veemente, Portuguese veemente, Spanish vehemente); or from Latin vehemēns (“vehement; very eager; ardent, furious, impetuous; emphatic”), probably from vē- (“lacking, too little”) + mēns (“mind; intellect; judgment, reasoning”).
vehement.g: Showing strong feelings; passionate; forceful or intense.

veil.e: From Middle English veil, veyl, from Anglo-Norman and Old Northern French veil (“sail, veil, shroud”) (Francien Old French voil, French voile), Latin vēlum (“cloth, covering”).
veil.g: Something hung up or spread out to hide or protect the face, or hide an object from view; usually of gauze, crepe, or similar diaphanous mat

vein.e: From Middle English veine, borrowed from Anglo-Norman veine, from Latin vēna (“a blood-vessel; vein; artery”) of uncertain origin.
vein.g: A blood vessel that transports blood from the capillaries back to the heart.

vengeance.e: From Anglo-Norman vengeaunce, from Old French vengeance, venjance, from vengier (“to avenge”). Analysable as venge + -ance.
vengeance.g: Revenge taken for an insult, injury, or other wrong.

venison.e: From Middle English venisoun, venesoun, from Anglo-Norman veneisun, venesoun, venesun (“meat of large game, particularly deer or boar; hunt”), from Latin vēnātiō, vēnātiōnem (“hunt; meat from a hunt”), formed on vēnātus, perfect participle of vēnor (“to hunt”).
venison.g: The meat of a deer, especially one that was hunted in its own natural habitat.

venom.e: From Middle English venym, from Old French venim, from Vulgar Latin *venīmen, from Early Medieval Latin venīnum, from Classical Latin venēnum (“drug; poison; a charm”), ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to love”).
venom.g: An animal toxin intended for defensive or offensive use; a biological poison delivered by bite, sting, etc., to protect an animal or to kill

venomous.e: From Middle English venymous, from Old French venimos, composed of venim (“venom”) + -os (adjective-forming suffix). Synchronically analysable as venom + -ous. Piecewise doublet of venenous.
venomous.g: Of an animal (specifically a snake) or parts of its body: producing venom (“a toxin intended for defensive or offensive use”) which is usual

vent.e: Partly from Middle French vent, from Latin ventus and partly from French éventer.
vent.g: An opening through which gases, especially air, can pass.

vent.e: From Spanish venta (“a poor inn, sale, market”).

venture.g: A risky or daring undertaking or journey.

verbal.e: From Old French verbal, from Late Latin verbālis (“belonging to a word”). Equivalent to verb + -al.

verdict.e: From Middle English verdit, from Anglo-Norman verdit (> Medieval Latin veredictum), from veir (“true”) + dit (“saying”); possibly a calque of a Germanic term such as Old English sōþword, sōþsprǣċ, sōþspell, sōþsagu, or sōþcwide, all meaning "true story, statement of truth, account, history".
verdict.g: A decision on an issue of fact in a civil or criminal case or an inquest.

verify.e: From Old French verifier (French: vérifier), from Medieval Latin vērificāre (“make true”), from Latin vērus (“true”) + faciō (“do, make”); see -fy.
verify.g: To substantiate or prove the truth of something.

verily.e: From Middle English verraily, from verray (“true, very”) + -ly.

verity.e: From Middle English verite, from Anglo-Norman verité or Middle French verité, from Old French verité, from Latin vēritās, from the adjective vērus (“true”).
verity.g: Truth, fact or reality, especially an enduring religious or ethical truth; veracity.

vermilion.e: From Middle English vermelioun, vermyloun, vermylon, vermilun, from Old French vermeillon (“vermilion”), from vermeil, from Latin vermiculus (“little worm”), from vermis (“worm”), ultimately in reference to Kermes vermilio, a type of scale insect used to make a crimson dye.
vermilion.g: A vivid red synthetic pigment made of mercury sulfide, cinnabar.

vermin.e: From Middle English vermyn, vermyne, from Old French vermine, from Vulgar Latin *verminum (“vermin”), collective noun formed from Latin vermis (“worm”).
vermin.g: Any of various common types of small insects or other animals which cause harm and annoyance.

verse.e: From Middle English vers, from a mixture of Old English fers and Old French vers; both from Latin versus (“a line in writing, and in poetry a verse; (originally) row, furrow”), from vertō (“to turn around”).
verse.g: A poetic form with regular meter and a fixed rhyme scheme.

verse.e: Back-formation from versus, misconstrued as a third-person singular verb verses.

version.e: Borrowed from Middle French version, from Medieval Latin versiō, from Latin vertō (“to turn”). Used in English since 16th century.
version.g: A specific form or variation of something.

very.e: From Middle English verray, from Old French verai (“true”), from Early Medieval Latin vērāgus, from Classical Latin vērāx, derived from vērus, from Proto-Italic *wēros, from Proto-Indo-European *weh₁ros. Distantly cognate with Old English wǣr (“true”).
very.g: To a great extent or degree.

vessel.e: From Middle English vessel, vessell (“small container”); from Old French vaissel (compare modern French vaisseau and Catalan vaixell), from Late Latin vāscellum, diminutive of vāsculum, diminutive of vās (“vase, vessel”).
vessel.g: A craft for transportation on or in water, air, or space.

vestment.e: From Middle English vestement, vestment, from Old French vestement, from Latin vestīmentum. By surface analysis, vest + -ment.
vestment.g: A robe, gown, or other article of clothing worn as an indication of office.

vestry.e: From Anglo-Norman vesterie, from Old French vestiaire (“room for vestments, dressing room”), from Latin vestiarium (“wardrobe”).
vestry.g: A room in a church where the clergy put on their vestments and where these are stored; also used for meetings and classes.

vesture.e: From Middle English vesture (noun) and vesturen (verb), from Anglo-Norman, from Old French vesteüre, from Vulgar Latin vestītūra (“clothing”), from Latin vestītus, perfect passive participle of vestiō (“to clothe”), from vestis (“garment”).
vesture.g: A covering of, or like, clothing.

vex.e: From Middle English vexen, from Old French vexer, from Latin vexāre (“disturb, agitate, annoy”).

vexation.e: From Late Middle English vexacioun, vexation (“physical suffering; act of inflicting trouble (specifically through unjustified legal action); anxiety, mental distress; mental disturbance”), from Anglo-Norman vexacion, vexation, Middle French vexacion, vexation (“distress, suffering.
vexation.g: The action of vexing, annoying, or irritating someone or something; (countable) an instance of this.

vexed.e: From Middle English vexed, vexede, vexit, vixid, equivalent to vex + -ed.
